intro: The best air purifier for mold is the IQAir HealthPro Plus, a sealed medical-grade unit whose HyperHEPA stage IQAir rates down to 0.003 microns, far below the 1 to 30 micron size of mold spores. For a musty smell, the Austin Air HealthMate Plus HM450 is the better buy because its filter carries roughly 15 pounds of carbon and zeolite, and the Winix 5500-2 is the value pick for a bedroom.

Spores are big by filter standards, so nearly any tightly built true HEPA unit with enough airflow for the room will pull them out of the air; the HEPA standard itself is 99.97 percent capture at 0.3 microns, the hardest size to catch. What separates the six below is airflow for the space, how much carbon they carry for odor, filter upkeep, and the absence of ozone gimmicks. The ranking draws on published CADR figures, AHAM Verified and CARB listings, maker specifications and patterns in owner feedback, not on lab trials of our own.
quickAnswer: Choose the IQAir HealthPro Plus if someone in the house has asthma or strong mold allergies, the Austin Air HealthMate Plus if a musty odor is the main problem, and the Levoit Core 600S or Winix 5500-2 for everyday allergy relief at a lower cost. Size by CADR, not the box's room claim, and fix the damp first: a purifier catches spores but never kills the colony.

sections.h: The 6 Best Air Purifiers for Mold in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: IQAir builds the HealthPro Plus for people who cannot tolerate leaky filtration. Air passes a coarse pre-filter, then a gas-phase stage of carbon and pellets for odors and chemicals, then a HyperHEPA stage IQAir rates for particles down to 0.003 microns. Mold spores are hundreds of times larger than that. Its cabinet is also gasketed so unfiltered air has no route around the media, something many lower-cost machines get wrong. The unit has a long record in clinics and hospitals, and owners with mold allergies and asthma are its most enthusiastic reviewers. The drawbacks are cost and size: it is the priciest unit on this list, it is heavy enough that it belongs on the floor of a living area rather than in a bedroom corner, and replacement media cost a lot, although IQAir's main HEPA stage is designed to last several years.
**Pros:** most thorough filtration here; sealed against bypass; separate pre-filter, gas and HEPA stages; long main-filter life.
**Cons:** premium price; large and heavy.

blocks.h3: Best for Musty Odor: Austin Air HealthMate Plus HM450

blocks.p: The musty smell in a damp basement is made of gases released by growing mold, and a HEPA filter does almost nothing for gases. That is where the HealthMate Plus stands apart. Austin Air packs roughly 15 pounds of activated carbon and zeolite around a medical-grade HEPA layer in one cartridge. Most purifiers carry a carbon sheet measured in ounces, so the difference for odor is large. The Plus model also uses carbon treated with potassium iodide to widen the range of chemicals it absorbs. Austin Air rates the filter for up to about five years, which keeps the yearly filter cost reasonable. The housing is steel and the control is a simple three-speed dial with nothing to pair or update. The trade-offs are bulk and noise: it is a large cylinder, and most owners run it on medium because high is loud.
**Pros:** very large carbon bed for odor; medical-grade HEPA; long filter life; all-steel build.
**Cons:** bulky and loud on high; no sensor, timer or app.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Austin+Air+HealthMate+Plus+HM450&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Large Rooms: Coway Airmega 400

blocks.p: The Airmega 400 draws air through both sides of the cabinet into two stacked filter sets, so it moves a lot of air without the fan sounding strained. Coway's room rating, which tops 1,000 square feet, is based on a single air change each hour. Spore control calls for several changes an hour, which puts its realistic range at roughly 500 to 800 square feet, the size of many finished basements and great rooms. Both filter stacks pair true HEPA media with a carbon layer. A particle sensor speeds the fan up in auto mode when readings climb, and the Smart model adds an app and filter-life tracking. Reviews from owners tend to mention quick results in large rooms and a hushed fan at the lower speeds. The carbon layer is thin next to dedicated odor units, so a strong musty smell improves but may linger, and replacement filter sets are a real ongoing cost.
**Pros:** strong airflow for open spaces; true HEPA plus carbon; auto mode with sensor; quiet on low.
**Cons:** modest carbon for heavy odor; filter sets are not cheap.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Coway+Airmega+400&tag=sktiger-20)

The 600S sits at the top of Levoit's Core range. Levoit puts its CADR at about 410 CFM, which gives a normal living room or primary bedroom several air changes per hour. Auto mode runs off a laser particle sensor, and the app logs readings over time, which makes it easy to spot a spike when someone leaves the basement door open or the dehumidifier stops. Levoit sells several replacement filters for it, including one marketed for mold and toxins with a heavier carbon blend. Owners commonly mention the quiet sleep mode and the value against premium brands. The weak points are small: the round tower pulls air from every side, so it wants open floor around it, and if you plan to leave it on auto the app is a nice extra rather than a reason to buy.
**Pros:** high CADR for its class; app with air quality history; mold-focused filter option; quiet sleep mode.
**Cons:** needs open floor space; app is optional for most users.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Levoit+Core+600S&tag=sktiger-20)

The 5500-2 has been a budget favorite for years for a simple reason: genuine true HEPA media and a washable carbon pre-filter at a price that still leaves money for a dehumidifier. AHAM lists it for a room of about 360 square feet, so think bedroom or small basement den. Auto mode reads particles and odor and adjusts the fan, and replacement filters are inexpensive. Its PlasmaWave feature is an ionizer that Winix says is CARB-certified to meet California's ozone emission limit, and it has its own off switch. Switch it off if anyone at home is sensitive to ozone; spore capture comes from the HEPA media, not the ionizer. Owners rate it well for value and longevity, with the usual note about fan noise on turbo.
**Pros:** true HEPA plus carbon pre-filter; low running cost; auto mode; ionizer can be switched off.
**Cons:** keep PlasmaWave off if ozone-sensitive; carbon is light for strong odor.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Winix+5500-2&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.h: Do Air Purifiers Help With Mold?

blocks.p: Yes, for spores in the air; no, for mold growing on surfaces.

An air purifier is a fan that pushes room air through filters. To earn the true HEPA label, a filter has to stop 99.97 percent of 0.3-micron particles, which is the hardest size to trap; bigger particles are caught at even higher rates. Mold spores typically measure 1 to 30 microns, so a sealed HEPA unit removes most of the spores that pass through it. That lowers what you breathe, and many people with mold allergies notice fewer symptoms within a week or two.

It cannot reach mold where it grows: on damp drywall, behind baseboards, under subfloors, in carpet pads. A purifier cleans only the air that flows into it, while a living colony keeps releasing new spores. Running a purifier without fixing the damp is like mopping under a dripping pipe.

ol: Control moisture, usually with a dehumidifier, and keep relative humidity below about 50 percent so mold stops spreading.
Clean or remove visible growth with proper protection.
Run a purifier to keep airborne spores down while the space dries and during cleanup, when disturbed mold sheds spores in large numbers.

blocks.p: If you have not found the moisture source yet, our guide on [how to fix a damp basement](/how-to-fix-a-damp-basement/) walks through the tests.

sections.h: Which Air Purifier Specs Matter for Mold?

blocks.p: Four numbers and one label decide whether a purifier is any good against mold.

CADR, or clean air delivery rate, is the volume of cleaned air a unit puts out each minute, rated separately for smoke, dust and pollen under the AHAM test. For mold, the dust and pollen figures are most relevant because spores fall in that size range. An AHAM Verified mark means an independent lab checked the number.

"HEPA-type", "HEPA-like" and "99 percent HEPA" are not the same standard. The spec you want reads 99.97 percent at 0.3 microns, or a medical-grade rating that meets it. A sealed housing with a gasket around the filter matters too, because air that bypasses the filter is not cleaned at all.

Musty odor is a gas, and only activated carbon removes it. Most compact purifiers carry a few ounces in a thin sheet that saturates quickly in a musty room. Odor-focused units carry pounds. If the maker does not list carbon weight, assume it is light.
California limits ozone from indoor air cleaners, and certified units meet that limit. Certification rules out the worst offenders. If a purifier has an ionizer, it should have an off switch.

sections.h: What Size Air Purifier Do You Need for Mold?

blocks.p: Size it by CADR, and size up. AHAM's guideline matches a unit to a room whose area is about one and a half times its smoke CADR. With 8-foot ceilings that comes to about five air changes an hour. For mold and allergies, aim for at least that.
Take your room's square footage and multiply by two-thirds. A 300 square foot bedroom wants a CADR of about 200 or more; a 600 square foot basement den wants about 400 or more.

blocks.p: Many coverage claims assume one air change per hour, fine for general freshness but too low for spores. If a box says 1,500 square feet, divide by three to four for a realistic mold-control area. This is the most common reason people decide purifiers do not work.

In a chopped-up or L-shaped basement, two mid-size units usually beat one big one in a corner, because each cleans its own zone. Low 7-foot ceilings stretch a given CADR further; vaulted ceilings need more than floor area suggests.

sections.h: Do UV-C Air Purifiers and Ionizers Kill Mold?

blocks.p: Not in any way that matters at home. Skip paying extra for them, and never use an ozone generator in an occupied house.

These are sold as mold killers. According to the EPA, ozone does little to mold at levels people can safely breathe, and the gas itself irritates airways and can make asthma worse. Professional ozone shock treatments of empty buildings exist, but that is not a household appliance. If you want an air purifier for mold with no ozone exposure, choose a sealed HEPA unit with no ionizer, or one whose ionizer you can switch off.

Ionizers charge particles so they stick to surfaces or collector plates, and some produce small amounts of ozone as a by-product. A CARB-certified ionizer with its own off switch, which many good purifiers have, is an acceptable middle ground. With asthma in the house, leave it off; the HEPA filter does the work regardless.

UV-C damages microorganisms in principle, but killing mold spores takes a large dose, and air passes a small internal lamp in a fraction of a second. Spores trapped on a dry HEPA filter are already out of the air and do not grow there. A sealed UV lamp in a certified unit is not harmful; it just is not worth paying more for.
Some of these can produce by-products such as formaldehyde under certain conditions. They add cost and uncertainty without fixing the real issue.
Do not add bleach or any chemical solution to a purifier or humidifier. Bleach fumes irritate the lungs, and no household purifier is designed for it.

sections.h: Will an Air Purifier Remove Mold Smell?

blocks.p: Only if it has a meaningful amount of activated carbon, and only for as long as the source is under control.

The musty smell is made of microbial volatile organic compounds, gases released by growing mold. HEPA filters trap particles, not gases, so a HEPA-only purifier can clear the spores and leave the smell untouched.

A thin carbon sheet handles light, occasional odor. A deep carbon bed measured in pounds, such as the roughly 15 pounds in the Austin Air HealthMate Plus, handles a persistent basement smell. The IQAir HealthPro Plus also has a dedicated gas-phase stage. The Coway, Levoit and Winix units help with moderate odor; Levoit sells a carbon-heavy mold and toxin filter for the 600S.
Carbon saturates. Once it does, it stops absorbing and the smell returns, even if the HEPA stage still has life left. If the musty smell comes back while the purifier is running, replace the carbon.

blocks.h3: Stop the smell at its source

blocks.p: The smell keeps coming as long as mold keeps growing. Bring humidity below about 50 to 60 percent, remove cardboard and old carpet, and clean small patches. When the odor survives dry air and new carbon, mold is still active somewhere hidden, such as inside a wall, under the floor or beside a slow pipe leak. Check suspect areas with a moisture meter.

sections.h: Air Purifier or Dehumidifier: Which Do You Need First?

blocks.p: If you can buy only one machine for a damp, musty basement, buy the dehumidifier. It removes the moisture mold needs, and spore production falls along with humidity over a few weeks. A purifier with no humidity control is always playing catch-up.

Buy the purifier first when moisture is already under control and symptoms persist, or when you need cleaner air in one room right now, such as a bedroom with a mold history, while the bigger fix is underway. People with mold allergies often run both for the first month after a cleanup.

blocks.h3: How they work across the year

blocks.p: Basements are usually drier in winter, so the dehumidifier may barely run. The purifier keeps catching dust and leftover spores all year, so it is the machine that stays on longer.

For a 1,000 square foot basement, a common setup is a 50-pint Energy Star dehumidifier plus a mid-size HEPA purifier with a CADR around 250 to 400. Our guide to the [best dehumidifier for basement](/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/) covers sizing and drain options.

ul: **Finished basement family room:** dehumidifier near the dampest wall or sump, large-room purifier near the seating.
**Bedroom over a damp crawlspace:** a mid-size true HEPA unit on low overnight, plus sealing gaps around pipes in the floor.
**Bathroom with mildew:** a purifier is the wrong tool; fix the exhaust fan and run it 20 to 30 minutes after showers.
**Unused storage basement:** a dehumidifier alone is usually enough. If basement air reaches the house through return ducts, a MERV 11 to 13 furnace filter helps if your system accepts it.

sections.h: Where Should You Put an Air Purifier for Mold, and How Long Should It Run?

blocks.p: Place it in the room you use most, which may not be the room where the mold turned up. If the family room is in the basement, put it there. When the basement is just storage and spores are drifting up the stairs, you breathe easier with the purifier in the bedroom or main living room. Leave roughly a foot of space on every side so nothing blocks the intake.

Spore levels climb back within an hour or two after a purifier switches off, especially where something is still releasing them. Leave it on auto, or on low overnight and higher during the day. Running costs on low are small for most units.

Run a purifier in or just outside the work area with the door closed, and keep it going for a day or two after you finish. Scrubbing, sanding or removing drywall releases a burst of spores. It does not replace an N95 or better respirator, which you should wear for any mold cleanup.
Keep them closed while it runs in humid weather. Outdoor air brings outdoor spores and, in summer, moisture that undoes the dehumidifier.

You cannot see spores, so judge by what you can observe: fewer morning symptoms, less congestion in the room, less dust on flat surfaces. A consumer particle monitor will not count spores, but it shows whether particle levels fall and how fast they rebound. At the first filter change, a gray HEPA filter is a good sign; one that looks barely used means the unit is too small, blocked or in a room with little air movement.

Clean pre-filters every two to four weeks in a basement, change HEPA filters on the maker's schedule or sooner after a cleanup, and bag old filters outdoors. Check replacement filter cost and availability before you buy; a filter that never gets changed turns any purifier into a fan.

sections.h: When Is Mold Too Big a Problem for an Air Purifier?

blocks.p: When it covers more than about 10 square feet, a patch roughly three feet by three feet. That is the point at which EPA guidance suggests professional help. Whatever the size, call a remediation contractor for mold in ductwork, mold behind finished walls after flooding, or any area touched by sewage.

Worsening asthma, frequent respiratory infections, or allergy symptoms that ease when you are away from home are reasons to see a doctor and consider a professional moisture and mold assessment. Finding the hidden source matters more than any filter.

Most basement moisture traces back to roof drainage, grading, plumbing or cracks in the foundation, and any decent contractor checks those before anything else. Our guide on [how to waterproof a basement](/how-to-waterproof-a-basement/) covers them in order.

blocks.h3: Be wary of test-first sales pitches

blocks.p: Indoor air always contains some spores, so an air test that finds spores proves little. What actually helps is locating wet materials and hidden growth, which a capable inspector does with a moisture meter, a light and, sometimes, an infrared camera. Treat any company that leads with air sampling and then quotes costly treatment from spore numbers alone with some skepticism.

mistakes: Trusting the room size on the box

The room size printed on a box usually means one air change per hour, enough to freshen a room but well short of what spores call for. A unit sold for 1,000 square feet may really clean about 300 square feet at the rate mold work needs. Size from CADR instead, aiming for at least two-thirds of the room's square footage.
Buying an ozone generator to kill mold

Ozone machines are sold to kill mold, yet at concentrations people can breathe safely they barely affect it, and the gas harms your lungs. The EPA advises against ozone generators in occupied spaces. Spend that money on a sealed true HEPA purifier and a dehumidifier, which actually lower spores and stop growth.
Expecting HEPA to remove the musty smell

The smell is a gas, and HEPA filters only catch particles. A carbon sheet a few millimeters thick saturates fast in a musty basement. Pick a model with pounds of carbon, and dry the space so the odor stops being made.
Running it only when the room smells

Spore levels climb back within hours of a purifier switching off, so turning it on only when the room smells means it always starts from behind. Leave it running around the clock on low or auto and bump the speed during cleanup or busy days.

A clogged filter moves less air, and a saturated carbon stage lets the odor come back. Owners often blame the purifier when the real problem is a filter that is months past due. Write the install date on the filter and budget for replacements when you buy the unit.
bottomLine: Most households get the relief they want from a Levoit Core 600S or a Winix 5500-2 matched to the room's square footage. Buy the Austin Air HealthMate Plus when odor bothers you more than sneezing, and the Coway Airmega 400 or Blueair 211+ when the space is a big, open basement. For asthma or a strong spore allergy, the IQAir HealthPro Plus is the most complete filtration you can put in a home. Whichever you choose, treat it as the last line of defense: dry the space below 50 percent humidity, clean or remove the growth, then let the purifier keep the air clear.

faqs.q: What is the best air purifier for mold?
faqs.a: The IQAir HealthPro Plus is the best air purifier for mold when filtration quality matters most, thanks to a sealed housing and a HyperHEPA stage rated to 0.003 microns. For a musty smell, the Austin Air HealthMate Plus and its roughly 15 pounds of carbon is the stronger pick. The Levoit Core 600S and Winix 5500-2 are the best values for everyday allergy relief.

faqs.q: Will a HEPA air purifier capture mold spores?
faqs.a: Yes. Mold spores measure roughly 1 to 30 microns, larger than the 0.3-micron particles a true HEPA filter is rated to stop 99.97 percent of. A sealed HEPA purifier sized for the room removes most airborne spores that pass through it. Growth on walls, wood or carpet is untouched, so you still have to clean the source.

faqs.q: Are there air purifiers that will remove mold smells?
faqs.a: Yes, if they carry enough activated carbon. The musty smell is a gas, which HEPA filters cannot catch. A model with pounds of carbon, like the Austin Air HealthMate Plus, keeps absorbing a stubborn smell long after a thin sheet would be spent. The smell only stops for good once humidity is under control and the growth is cleaned up.

faqs.q: Do UV light air purifiers kill mold?
faqs.a: Not to any useful degree. A small UV-C lamp inside a purifier has little effect on mold spores because air rushes past it too quickly for a lethal dose. Spores trapped on a HEPA filter are already out of the air. A sealed UV lamp in a certified unit is not harmful, but the HEPA filter does the real work, so do not pay extra for UV.

faqs.q: Should an air purifier run all day for mold?
faqs.a: Yes, run it continuously. Within an hour or two of switching off, airborne spores are back near where they started, faster still if anything is growing. Use auto mode, or low overnight and a higher speed during the day and during cleanup. Most purifiers use little electricity on low, so continuous running costs little.

faqs.q: Is a dehumidifier or air purifier better for mold?
faqs.a: A dehumidifier is better for preventing mold, because it removes the moisture mold needs to grow. A purifier then catches spores already in the air and helps with allergy symptoms. In a damp basement, buy the dehumidifier first and keep humidity below about 50 percent. If symptoms continue after that, add a HEPA purifier.

faqs.q: Can an air purifier replace mold remediation?
faqs.a: No. A purifier only treats the air; colonies on drywall, framing or carpet go on shedding new spores until they are cleaned or removed. Clean small areas yourself with the right product and an N95 respirator. Hire a qualified remediation contractor for anything over about 10 square feet, for mold in ductwork, and for anything after sewage or flood water.
